core: working definition (CDC-attributed): transmission-based precautions are the second tier of basic infection control, used IN ADDITION to standard precautions for patients who may be infected or colonized with certain infectious agents for which additional precautions are needed to prevent infection transmission — the added measures used when standard precautions are not enough, chosen by how the germ travels
the three types named: contact, droplet, and airborne — each with one line and an original example of when it applies

contact precautions: gloves and gowns for interactions that may involve contact with the patient or the patient's environment, dedicated or cleaned patient-care equipment, prioritized room cleaning — with an original example
droplet precautions: mask donned on room entry and worn within close range of the patient, mask on the patient during transport — with an original example
airborne precautions: fit-tested NIOSH-approved N95 or higher respirator plus an airborne infection isolation room (negative pressure) — with an original example, stated simply
when they end: duration depends on the infection and its treatment, not on a fixed number of days (CDC 2007 guideline Appendix A type-and-duration table) — stated simply
honest framing: precautions are matched to the germ's travel plan — the reality check
supporting: CDC 2007 Isolation Guideline V.A.1: in addition to standard precautions, use transmission-based precautions for patients with documented or suspected infection or colonization with highly transmissible or epidemiologically important pathogens

Droplet separation: patients sharing a room are physically separated by more than 3 feet (2007 guideline V.C.2.a.iv); droplet pathogens are large-particle respiratory droplets (>5 microns) generated by coughing, sneezing, or talking (V.C.1)

Duration examples from Appendix A: meningococcal disease droplet precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy; major draining abscess contact precautions until drainage stops or is contained by a dressing; V.A.2 extends duration for immunosuppressed patients with prolonged viral shedding

OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing 10.2: gowns are used for patients on contact and droplet precautions; healthcare workers wear a mask when caring for a patient on droplet precautions; an N95 respirator, when properly fitted, protects the wearer from very small particles that float in the air such as tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, and COVID-19

claims.claim: Transmission-based precautions are the second tier of basic infection control, used in addition to standard precautions for patients who may be infected or colonized with certain infectious agents for which additional precautions are needed to prevent infection transmission.

The CDC identifies three categories of transmission-based precautions — contact, droplet, and airborne — and the category is chosen according to how the germ is transmitted (touching, respiratory droplets, or the airborne route).

Contact precautions are used for patients with known or suspected infections that represent an increased risk for contact transmission; healthcare personnel wear a gown and gloves for all interactions that may involve contact with the patient or the patient's environment, use disposable or dedicated patient-care equipment (e.g., blood pressure cuffs) where possible, and prioritize cleaning and disinfection of the patient's room.

Droplet precautions are used for patients known or suspected to be infected with pathogens transmitted by respiratory droplets generated by coughing, sneezing, or talking; healthcare personnel don a mask upon entry into the patient room or space, patients wear a mask when transported outside the room, and patients sharing a room are physically separated by more than 3 feet.

Airborne precautions are used for patients known or suspected to be infected with pathogens transmitted by the airborne route (e.g., tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, disseminated herpes zoster); the patient is placed in an airborne infection isolation room (AIIR) and healthcare personnel wear a fit-tested NIOSH-approved N95 or higher level respirator.

The duration of transmission-based precautions depends on the infection and its treatment rather than on a fixed number of days: the CDC's isolation guideline Appendix A lists per-condition durations — meningococcal disease keeps droplet precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy, a major draining abscess keeps contact precautions until drainage stops or is contained by a dressing, and precautions may be extended for immunosuppressed patients with prolonged viral shedding.

Transmission-based precautions are layered on top of standard precautions, which continue to apply to all patient care; the two tiers of recommended precautions are standard precautions for all patient care and transmission-based precautions added for patients with known or suspected infections.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What airborne precautions require when a negative-pressure room is not available
positions: CDC transmission-based precautions page: place the patient in an airborne infection isolation room (AIIR); when AIIRs cannot be implemented due to limited engineering resources, masking the patient and placing them in a private room with the door closed reduces risk until transfer
The classic 2007 guideline frames the AIIR as the standard placement for airborne precautions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the standard: a fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator plus a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room, with one line noting that facilities without such a room use interim measures (patient masked, door closed) until transfer. Stated simply, per the assignment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact 'distance' wording for droplet spread
positions: 2007 guideline: patients sharing a room are physically separated by more than 3 feet
The current CDC page emphasizes masking on room entry without repeating a distance figure
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says droplets travel a short distance — roughly within about three feet — and that the mask goes on at the door regardless of exact distance, citing both the guideline's separation rule and the page's masking rule.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which diseases belong in which category can shift as guidance is updated
positions: Appendix A of the 2007 guideline was updated in September 2018
Newer pathogens (e.g., COVID-19) have had evolving recommendations across guideline versions
Classic examples (TB, measles, chickenpox for airborne; influenza for droplet; MRSA wounds and C. difficile for contact) appear consistently across versions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only stable, long-standing examples that appear consistently across guideline versions, and notes in the reality-check section that guidance can be updated as evidence grows — the travel-plan question stays the same.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-4 generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Transmission-Based Precautions is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations') with no clinical content — no definition, no categories, no PPE specifics. Nothing in it survived the rewrite.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generic draft with a source-verified lesson: working definition attributed to the CDC, the three categories (contact, droplet, airborne) verified against the CDC transmission-based precautions page and the 2007 Isolation Precautions Guideline, duration logic verified against the guideline's Appendix A type-and-duration table, PPE specifics corroborated by OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing 10.2, and the two-tier layering framing verified against the CDC infection-control-basics page.
